subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If a > b > 0 and 0 < x < π, and f(x) = (a² − b²)^(−1/2) cos⁻¹((a cos x + b)/(a + b cos x)), show that f′(x) = 1/(a + b cos x).

mark_split.label: Substitute the half angle form of cos x
Turn the inverse cosine into an inverse tangent
Simplify back to a + b cos x

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.208, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Long Answer question 12. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. STEM: the printed constraint line reached this desk garbled, as "0 < π > x", which is not a usable condition. The stem was authored as 0 < x < π. That is the condition the working actually requires and the only reading consistent with the rest of the question: it makes sin x > 0, which is what removes the modulus from √(sin²x) in the differentiation, and it makes tan(x/2) > 0, which is what puts the half angle inside the principal range. The book was not otherwise consulted and no printed solution was read. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a CHAPTER-level marks banner (8M + 4M + 2 × 2M = 16M) but no per-step allocation on any answer. The split follows the shape this bank uses for a Maths-1B Section C question. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. Paper position: Maths-1B Section C runs Q19 to Q21 at 8 marks each, answer any 2 of 3, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The mathematics was checked independently before writing, in two parts and with three parameter pairs, (a, b) = (3, 1), (5, 2) and (2, 1.5). First the half angle identity: Cos⁻¹((a cos x + b)/(a + b cos x)) and 2 Tan⁻¹(√((a − b)/(a + b))·tan(x/2)) agreed to nine decimal places at x = 1 and x = 2 for every pair. Then the derivative: f was differentiated as a central difference quotient at x = 0.5, 1, 2 and 2.8, and all twelve values matched 1/(a + b cos x) — for example a = 3, b = 1, x = 1 gives 0.282461754 both ways, and a = 2, b = 1.5, x = 2.8 gives 1.704545971 both ways. steps.why: The argument of the inverse cosine is a ratio of two expressions that are linear in cos x. Writing cos x in the half angle form makes both of them ratios with the same denominator 1 + t², which then cancels, and that is what reveals the standard form underneath.
common_mistakes: Cancelling cos x between a cos x + b and a + b cos x, which are sums and have no common factor.
Using cos x = 1 − 2sin²(x/2), which halves the angle but does not put both parts over the same denominator.
steps.memory_tip: The half angle substitution t = tan(x/2) turns any ratio of polynomials in sin x and cos x into a ratio of polynomials in t. It is the standard move when cos x appears both on top and underneath.
